concepts.title: Kinematics: blunt versus penetrating
key_points: Kinematics is working out what the body absorbed from how the incident happened
Energy is transferred to tissue and that transfer is what causes injury — speed matters far more than weight
Blunt trauma spreads energy over a wide area, so injuries are often internal with little to see outside
Penetrating trauma concentrates energy along a path, so the damage follows the track of the object
A small external wound in penetrating trauma says nothing about the internal damage
Look for the three collisions in a vehicle: vehicle into object, occupant into vehicle, organs into the inside of the body
Examine the scene as well as the patient — a starred windscreen, a bent steering wheel, a deformed door tell you where the energy went
Kinematics raises or lowers your index of suspicion; it never replaces assessment
misconceptions: Assuming a patient is uninjured because there is nothing to see
Judging a stab wound by the size of the hole
Not looking at the vehicle before it is towed
Using mechanism alone to decide a patient is fine
exam_favorites: Why a small penetrating wound means little

read.plain:
Kinematics is the study of what happened to the body, worked out from what happened to everything else. You are reconstructing where the energy went.

The principle is that injury is energy transferred into tissue. And of the two things that determine how much energy there is, speed matters far more than weight. Doubling the mass roughly doubles the energy; doubling the speed multiplies it by about four. A small car at high speed carries more energy than a large car at low speed, and that is why speed dominates every mechanism discussion.

Blunt trauma spreads that energy across a wide area. Nothing breaks the skin, the force goes through, and organs decelerate, tear, shear and bleed inside a body that looks untouched. This is what makes blunt trauma dangerous to assess: the outside can be almost normal while a spleen is bleeding.

Penetrating trauma does the opposite. It concentrates energy along a narrow path, and the damage follows that path. Which gives you a useful question — what is on the line between the entry point and wherever the object stopped?

And here is the thing people get wrong constantly: the size of the external wound tells you nothing. A knife wound may be a centimetre across and have gone through a lung, a diaphragm and a liver. Never be reassured by a small hole.

For vehicle crashes, think in three collisions. First, the vehicle hits something and stops. Second, the occupant keeps moving and hits the inside of the vehicle — windscreen, wheel, dashboard, door. Third, and the one that gets forgotten, the organs keep moving and hit the inside of the body. That third collision is where the aorta tears and the brain strikes the skull, and there is nothing to see from outside.

Which is why you look at the vehicle. A starred windscreen means a head hit it. A bent steering wheel means a chest did. An intruding door means the energy came in sideways at somebody's chest and pelvis. Look before it gets towed, because that information is not available later and it genuinely changes what the hospital looks for.

One caution to finish. Kinematics moves your index of suspicion up or down. It never replaces assessment. A terrible-looking crash can produce an uninjured patient and a trivial one can kill. You use the mechanism to decide how hard to look — not to decide what you will find.
read.standard: Kinematics comprises analysis of energy transfer to tissue derived from incident mechanics. Kinetic energy varies with the square of velocity and linearly with mass, rendering velocity the dominant determinant. Blunt trauma distributes energy across a broad surface, producing internal injury with minimal external evidence through deceleration, shearing and compression. Penetrating trauma concentrates energy along a trajectory, with injury following the path of the projectile or implement; external wound dimensions correlate poorly with internal damage. Vehicular trauma is analysed as three sequential collisions: vehicle with object, occupant with vehicle interior, and viscera with the internal body structures, the last producing aortic disruption and cerebral injury without external signs. Vehicle inspection for windscreen starring, steering wheel deformation and compartment intrusion identifies energy distribution and is unavailable after recovery. Kinematic analysis modifies index of suspicion and does not substitute for assessment.

eli_new.analogy: Energy has to go somewhere. Kinematics is following it from the bumper, through the windscreen, into the patient, and then into the organs that kept moving after the patient stopped.
eli_new.body: The third collision is the one nobody pictures. The car stops, then the person stops, and then — a fraction of a second later — the organs stop, by hitting the inside of the body. Nothing about that is visible from outside, which is exactly why mechanism matters.

Blunt spreads energy widely, often with little to see outside

story.title: Not a mark on him
story.dispatch: Engine 3 — single vehicle into a wall, driver out and walking.
story.body:
He was on the verge, apologetic, entirely uninjured to look at, and quite keen for everybody to go home.

The officer walked round the car anyway and found the steering wheel bent forward and a starred windscreen.

Something had hit both of those hard enough to deform them, and that something had been him.

concepts.title: Mechanism-based index of suspicion
key_points: Index of suspicion is how strongly you expect injury before you have found any
It comes from the mechanism, the patient's age and health, and what the scene shows you
Certain mechanisms raise it sharply: ejection, death of another occupant in the same vehicle, a fall from height, rollover, intrusion into the compartment, and being struck as a pedestrian
The specific thresholds for significant mechanism vary between systems and are set by local trauma triage criteria — use yours
Older patients and children are injured by less energy than a healthy adult, so the same mechanism means more in them
Patients on anticoagulants sustain more serious bleeding from the same mechanism
A high index of suspicion changes what you do: more thorough assessment, earlier transport decision, and saying it out loud at handover
The absence of complaint does not lower the index of suspicion, because distracting injuries and adrenaline both mask pain
misconceptions: Lowering suspicion because the patient says they are fine
Applying adult thresholds to a child or an older patient
Quoting a height or speed threshold from memory instead of the local criteria
Failing to mention the mechanism at handover
exam_favorites: What raises the index of suspicion
Why age changes the same mechanism
Not lowering suspicion on a patient's say-so

read.plain:
Index of suspicion is the expectation you carry before you have found anything. It is not a guess; it is a deliberate position you take based on the mechanism, the patient, and the scene.

Some mechanisms raise it sharply. Ejection from a vehicle. Another occupant in the same vehicle who died. A significant fall. A rollover. Intrusion into the passenger compartment. A pedestrian struck by a vehicle. A motorcyclist separated from the machine. Each of those tells you a large amount of energy was available.

Now, you will have noticed I have not given you numbers — no fall heights, no speeds, no intrusion measurements. That is deliberate. Those thresholds genuinely differ between systems, and they get revised. Your service has trauma triage criteria with specific figures in them and those figures are the ones that matter for your destination decisions. Learn yours, from your own protocol, rather than from a number somebody half-remembers from a different state.

The patient changes the meaning of the mechanism, and this is where real judgement comes in.

Older patients are injured by less energy. Bones are more brittle, tissues less elastic, and the reserve to compensate is smaller. A fall from standing height — which in a young adult is nothing — is a genuinely significant mechanism in an eighty-year-old. It is one of the commonest ways older people sustain serious injury, and it barely registers as a mechanism if you are thinking in terms of road speeds.

Children are different again. They are smaller, so the same energy is distributed through less body, and their organs sit closer together. They also compensate extremely well and then fall apart suddenly.

And anticoagulants change everything, as covered elsewhere: the same mechanism, much more bleeding.

So what does a high index of suspicion actually change? Three things. You assess more thoroughly and you look for things you have not been told about. You make your transport decision earlier rather than waiting to be convinced. And you say it out loud at handover — 'ejected', 'fatality in the same vehicle', 'fall from standing on a blood thinner'. That sentence changes how the receiving team meets you.

One last point, and it is the one that catches people. A patient saying they feel fine does not lower the index of suspicion. Adrenaline is a powerful painkiller for the first half hour. A dramatic, obvious injury distracts from a quiet serious one. People walk around on fractured spines. Believe the mechanism over the reassurance.
read.standard: Index of suspicion denotes anticipatory expectation of injury derived from mechanism, patient factors and scene findings, established prior to examination. Mechanisms conferring elevated suspicion include ejection, death of another occupant within the same vehicle, falls, rollover, compartment intrusion, pedestrian and motorcyclist impacts. Specific numerical thresholds defining significant mechanism vary between systems and are established by local trauma triage criteria, which govern destination decisions. Geriatric patients sustain injury at lower energy owing to reduced bone density, decreased tissue elasticity and diminished physiological reserve; ground-level falls constitute significant mechanism in this population. Paediatric patients distribute energy through smaller body mass with closer organ proximity and compensate effectively prior to abrupt decompensation. Anticoagulation increases haemorrhage severity for equivalent mechanism. Elevated index of suspicion alters assessment thoroughness, transport timing and handover content. Absence of patient complaint does not reduce index of suspicion owing to catecholamine-mediated analgesia and distracting injury.

eli_new.analogy: Index of suspicion is how hard you are prepared to look before anybody has given you a reason. The mechanism buys that willingness; the patient's reassurance does not sell it back.
eli_new.body: The mechanism people underrate most is a fall from standing height in an older person. It sounds like nothing next to a road crash, and it is one of the most common ways older patients are seriously hurt.

story.title: Off the bottom step
story.dispatch: Medic 1 — 82-year-old female, fall at home, sitting up talking.
story.body:
She had missed the bottom step and landed on the hall floor. A metre, at most. It did not sound like a mechanism at all.

The crew treated it as one, because she was 82 and on an anticoagulant.

A fall from standing is one of the most common ways older people are seriously injured, and it barely registers if you are thinking in road speeds.

concepts.title: Trauma triage and destination
key_points: Not every injured patient needs a trauma centre, and not every hospital can manage major trauma
Trauma triage criteria decide destination, and they are set locally — learn yours specifically
Criteria are usually tiered: physiological findings first, then anatomical injuries, then mechanism, then special patient factors
Physiological criteria come first because a patient who is abnormal now is the most urgent regardless of what caused it
Anatomical criteria are specific injuries that need trauma centre resources, such as penetrating injury to the torso or two or more long bone fractures
Mechanism criteria come third, and they catch patients who look well but were exposed to major energy
Special considerations include age, anticoagulation, pregnancy and burns, and they can move a patient up a tier
Under-triage — taking a major trauma patient to the wrong hospital — is more harmful than over-triage, so the criteria are deliberately cautious
Time to definitive care is what matters, so a longer drive to the right hospital usually beats a short drive to the wrong one
misconceptions: Taking a major trauma patient to the nearest hospital because it is nearer
Applying criteria from memory rather than from the local protocol
Ignoring the special-considerations tier in older or pregnant patients
Treating over-triage as an equal error to under-triage

read.plain:
Two facts sit under this whole concept. Not every injured patient needs a trauma centre — sending everybody would swamp the system and help nobody. And not every hospital can manage major trauma; some do not have a surgeon in the building overnight.

So there are criteria that decide where a patient goes. They are set locally, they vary, and they are revised. Learn yours specifically, from your own protocol.

What is consistent is the structure. The criteria come in tiers, checked in order.

First, physiological. What are the vital signs and the level of consciousness doing right now? A patient who is hypotensive, or breathing badly, or has a reduced level of consciousness goes to a trauma centre regardless of what caused it. This tier is first because being abnormal now outranks every theory about mechanism.

Second, anatomical. Specific injuries that need resources only a trauma centre has: penetrating injury to the head, neck, torso or proximal limbs; two or more long bone fractures; a flail chest; a suspected pelvic fracture; an amputation; paralysis. The patient may look stable, but the injury named is one that needs a surgeon.

Third, mechanism. This tier catches the patient who is physiologically normal, has no obvious named injury, and was exposed to an enormous amount of energy. Ejection, a death in the same vehicle, a significant fall. They may well be fine. Some of them are not, and this tier exists for those.

Fourth, special considerations. Age — both ends. Anticoagulation. Pregnancy. Burns. Anything that means this patient tolerates injury worse than the tier they landed in suggests. This tier moves people up, and it is the one most often skipped.

Now the asymmetry that explains why the criteria are deliberately over-inclusive. Over-triage means taking somebody to a trauma centre who turned out not to need it. Cost: resources, and a longer journey for that patient. Under-triage means taking a major trauma patient somewhere that cannot manage them. Cost: a transfer that wastes the hour that mattered most, and sometimes a death.

Those two errors are not equivalent, and the criteria are written knowing that. A degree of over-triage is designed in, on purpose. If you are hesitating between the two, the system's own logic says go to the trauma centre.

Which answers the question about distance. Nearest is not automatically right. What matters is time to definitive care — to a surgeon, an operating theatre, blood. A longer drive to a hospital that can provide that usually beats a shorter drive to one that will have to arrange a transfer. There are exceptions, chiefly an airway you cannot manage, and those exceptions are in your protocol too.
read.standard: Trauma triage criteria determine destination and are established locally with substantial inter-system variation. Criteria are conventionally structured in sequential tiers. Physiological criteria — abnormal vital signs and reduced level of consciousness — are assessed first, as current physiological derangement supersedes mechanistic inference. Anatomical criteria comprise specific injuries requiring trauma centre resources: penetrating injury to head, neck, torso or proximal extremities; multiple long bone fractures; flail chest; suspected pelvic fracture; amputation; and neurological deficit. Mechanism criteria identify physiologically normal patients exposed to substantial energy transfer. Special consideration criteria — age extremes, anticoagulation, pregnancy, burns — escalate triage tier and are the most frequently omitted. Under-triage carries substantially greater harm than over-triage, as inter-facility transfer consumes the interval of greatest therapeutic value; criteria are therefore deliberately over-inclusive. Destination selection is governed by time to definitive care rather than geographical proximity, with unmanageable airway constituting the principal exception per local protocol.

eli_new.analogy: Over-triage costs a longer journey. Under-triage costs the hour that mattered. The criteria are written knowing those are not the same mistake.
eli_new.body: The tier people skip is the fourth one. A patient who does not meet physiological, anatomical or mechanism criteria but is 88 and on an anticoagulant is not a low-acuity patient, and that tier exists to catch exactly them.

story.title: Fourteen minutes further
story.dispatch: Medic 3 — motorcyclist versus car, patient conscious and talking.
story.body:
His vital signs were normal, he was making jokes, and the local hospital was six minutes away.

He had an open femur fracture and had been separated from the bike at speed, and the trauma centre was twenty minutes.

They drove the twenty. Under-triage costs an hour of transfer; over-triage costs fourteen minutes of driving.

Age at either extreme, anticoagulated, pregnant, burns?
Trauma centre per local criteria. Pre-alert.

concepts.title: The golden period and the platinum ten minutes
key_points: The golden period is the idea that outcomes in major trauma depend on how quickly definitive care is reached
Definitive care usually means surgery and blood, and neither is available in an ambulance
The historical figure of one hour is a useful teaching idea rather than a precise biological threshold, and the modern framing is simply that time matters
The platinum ten minutes is the target for scene time in major trauma: aim to be moving within about ten minutes
On-scene time is spent only on what cannot be done in a moving ambulance
Airway, catastrophic bleeding control and extrication are scene tasks; almost everything else can be done en route
Load and go is not the opposite of good care, it is what good care looks like when the problem is inside the abdomen
Long scene times in major trauma are usually caused by doing sequentially what could be done simultaneously, or by procedures that could wait
misconceptions: Completing a full secondary survey on scene in major trauma
Treating the one hour as a precise deadline
Delaying transport for interventions that could be done en route
Confusing speed with rushing — the goal is efficiency, not panic
exam_favorites: What belongs on scene and what belongs en route

read.plain:
The golden period is the idea that in major trauma, outcome depends heavily on how fast the patient reaches definitive care.

Start with what definitive care means, because the concept is meaningless without it. For a patient bleeding inside their abdomen, definitive care is a surgeon stopping the bleeding and blood replacing what was lost. That is it. It is not oxygen, not a splint, not a cannula, and not anything an ambulance carries. Which means every minute on scene is a minute the actual treatment is not happening.

You will hear it called the golden hour, and it is worth being honest about that number. It came from observation rather than from a biological threshold, and it has been debated for decades. Nobody becomes unsalvageable at sixty-one minutes. The modern framing is more sensible: for a bleeding trauma patient, time matters, less of it is better, and there is no threshold below which delay stops costing anything.

The platinum ten minutes is the practical half. It is a target for scene time in major trauma — aim to have the patient moving within about ten minutes of your arrival.

That sounds impossible until you apply the rule that makes it work: on scene, do only what cannot be done in a moving ambulance.

What cannot: managing an airway that is failing now. Stopping catastrophic external bleeding. Getting the patient physically out of the wreckage. Those are scene tasks and they are why you are on scene at all.

What can: a full set of vital signs, splinting most things, bandaging most things, the secondary survey, a detailed history, getting a name and date of birth. All of it works fine at fifty kilometres an hour.

Load and go has a bad reputation, as though it means abandoning care. It does not. It means recognising that for this particular patient the treatment is elsewhere, and everything you can do is done better while travelling towards it. Careful, complete assessment on scene is right for many patients. For the one bleeding internally, it is the wrong choice made carefully.

And when scene times run long in major trauma, the cause is usually one of two things. Either tasks are being done one after another that three people could do simultaneously, or somebody is doing a procedure that would work just as well in ten minutes' time. Neither is about speed of movement. The answer is not to rush — rushing causes errors — it is to work in parallel and to leave the deferrable things for the journey.
read.standard: The golden period denotes the relationship between time to definitive care and outcome in major trauma. Definitive care comprises surgical haemorrhage control and blood product administration, neither available prehospitally; scene time therefore represents delay to the only effective intervention. The traditional one-hour figure derives from observational origins rather than a defined physiological threshold and is best understood as a teaching construct; contemporary framing holds that time to definitive care matters continuously without a discrete threshold. The platinum ten minutes denotes a target scene interval of approximately ten minutes in major trauma. Scene interventions are restricted to those impossible during transport: airway management, control of catastrophic external haemorrhage and extrication. Assessment, splinting, bandaging, vital signs and history are performed en route. Prolonged scene times typically result from sequential rather than parallel task performance, or from deferrable procedures performed prematurely; the remedy is parallel working rather than increased speed of movement.

eli_new.analogy: The treatment for a bleeding abdomen is in an operating theatre. Everything you do on scene happens somewhere the treatment is not.
eli_new.body: Load and go is not the opposite of thorough care. For a patient bleeding internally, a careful complete scene assessment is the wrong decision made carefully. Do the three things that cannot wait, and do everything else while moving.

story.title: Eleven minutes on scene
story.dispatch: Debrief — penetrating abdominal injury, scene time review.
story.body:
Everything had been done correctly. Full set of vitals, complete secondary survey, a splint on a forearm, and a careful handover prepared.

All of it was good care and all of it could have happened in the back of a moving ambulance.

Nobody had rushed, and nobody had made a mistake. The eleven minutes were the mistake.

concepts.title: External bleeding control
key_points: Arterial bleeding is bright red and spurts with the pulse; venous is darker and flows steadily; capillary oozes
Catastrophic external bleeding is managed before the airway, because it kills faster than anything else you can fix
Direct pressure is the first and most effective intervention, and it works when it is firm, focused on one point, and held
Pressure that is spread over a wide dressing is weaker than pressure focused on the bleeding point
Do not lift the dressing to look — every time you do, you tear apart what was forming
If blood soaks through, add dressings on top and press harder; do not remove what is already there
For a limb where direct pressure fails or is impractical, move to a tourniquet without hesitating
For a junctional wound — groin, armpit, neck — where a tourniquet cannot go, pack the wound and press
Elevation and pressure points are no longer taught as primary measures; direct pressure, packing and tourniquets are the sequence
misconceptions: Lifting the dressing to check whether the bleeding has stopped
Spreading pressure across a large bulky dressing instead of focusing it
Removing a soaked dressing and starting again
Working through the airway first when the patient is exsanguinating
Delaying a tourniquet to try direct pressure for longer than it is working
exam_favorites: The direct pressure, packing, tourniquet sequence

read.plain:
Three kinds of bleeding, told apart by colour and behaviour. Arterial is bright red and spurts in time with the pulse, because it is coming from a pressurised vessel. Venous is darker and flows steadily. Capillary oozes from a graze and usually stops itself.

Now the one thing that reorders everything you have learned about priorities. Normally the sequence is airway, then breathing, then circulation. Catastrophic external bleeding comes before all of it. A patient with a severed femoral artery has a few minutes; a patient with an obstructed airway has a few more. If blood is pouring out of somebody, you stop that first and then go back to the airway.

Direct pressure is the first intervention and the most effective, and the reason it sometimes fails is that it is done badly. Three things make it work.

Firm. Not resting a hand on a dressing — pressing, hard enough that it takes effort to keep it up, hard enough that you will want to swap over after a few minutes.

Focused. Pressure on one point, over the bleeding vessel. A thick fluffy dressing spreads your force over a wide area and dilutes it. Two fingertips on the actual bleeding point beat a palm on a wad of gauze.

And held. This is the one people fail. Clotting takes time and every time you lift the dressing to check, you pull apart what was forming and start the clock again. Do not look. If you need to know whether it is working, look at the patient and look at whether fresh blood is appearing at the edges.

If blood soaks through, add on top and press harder. Do not peel the first dressing off — anything that was forming comes away with it.

When direct pressure is not working, or cannot practically be applied, escalate. On a limb: tourniquet, and do not agonise over the decision. For a junctional wound where a limb tourniquet cannot reach — the groin, the armpit, the neck — pack the wound and hold pressure on the packing.

One piece of unlearning. Elevation and pressure points were taught as intermediate steps for many years. They are no longer taught as primary measures, because the evidence for them was poor and the time spent on them delayed things that work. The sequence now is direct pressure, packing, tourniquet. If someone senior tells you to elevate, elevating a limb harms nobody — but do not let it substitute for pressure that is working or a tourniquet that is needed.
read.standard: External haemorrhage is classified by source: arterial bleeding is bright red and pulsatile; venous bleeding is darker and continuous; capillary bleeding oozes. Catastrophic external haemorrhage precedes airway management in the assessment sequence, as exsanguination produces death more rapidly than airway obstruction. Direct pressure constitutes the primary intervention; efficacy requires that pressure be firm, focused over the bleeding point rather than distributed across bulky dressings, and sustained without interruption. Dressing removal disrupts forming clot; saturated dressings are supplemented rather than replaced, with increased pressure. Where direct pressure fails or is impractical on an extremity, tourniquet application follows without delay. Junctional wounds not amenable to tourniquet — inguinal, axillary, cervical — require wound packing with sustained pressure. Elevation and pressure point compression are no longer taught as primary measures owing to limited supporting evidence and the delay they introduce; the current sequence is direct pressure, packing, tourniquet.

eli_new.analogy: Pressure is not a gesture. It is a job that makes your arms ache, focused on one square centimetre, held without looking for far longer than feels necessary.
eli_new.body: The most common reason direct pressure fails is that somebody keeps lifting it to check. Clot formation is not instant, and every look starts the process again. Press, and do not look.

story.title: Every thirty seconds
story.dispatch: Engine 7 — laceration to the forearm, heavy bleeding, bystander first aid in progress.
story.body:
A well-meaning bystander had a dressing on it and was lifting the corner every thirty seconds to see whether it had stopped.

It had not stopped. It had been starting to stop, twelve separate times.

The firefighter put two fingers on one spot, pressed hard, and did not move for six minutes.

concepts.title: Tourniquet application
key_points: A tourniquet is the correct treatment for life-threatening limb bleeding that direct pressure has not controlled, and for an amputation
Modern practice is that tourniquets are safe when applied properly and the old fear of losing the limb is out of proportion to the risk
Apply high and tight above the wound, over a single bone where possible, and never over a joint
Tighten until the bleeding stops and the distal pulse is gone — a tourniquet that has not stopped the bleeding is too loose
A tourniquet that is too loose can make bleeding worse, because it blocks venous return without stopping arterial inflow
It will hurt, and that pain is expected — it is not a reason to loosen it
Never cover a tourniquet, and write the time of application somewhere visible, on the tourniquet or on the patient
Once applied, do not remove or loosen it in the field — release is a hospital decision
If one tourniquet does not stop the bleeding, apply a second just above the first
misconceptions: Applying it too loosely, which increases bleeding
Removing or loosening it because the patient is in pain
Covering it with a blanket so the receiving team does not see it
Applying it over a joint
Not recording the time of application
exam_favorites: High and tight, never over a joint
Tighten until the distal pulse is gone
Record the time and never cover it

read.plain:
A tourniquet stops life-threatening bleeding from a limb. It is indicated when direct pressure has not controlled the bleeding, when direct pressure is impractical — multiple casualties, a hazardous scene, a patient who has to be moved now — and immediately for a traumatic amputation.

The historical reluctance is worth addressing, because it still lingers. For a long time tourniquets were taught as a desperate last resort that would cost the limb. That belief came from poor devices, applied badly, and left on for extremely long periods. Modern practice, informed by a great deal of military experience, is that a properly applied tourniquet is safe for hours and that the risk of losing a limb is far smaller than the risk of bleeding to death. Patients die from delayed tourniquets. They very rarely lose limbs to prompt ones.

Application. High and tight above the wound. Over a single bone where you can — upper arm or thigh — because a tourniquet across two bones may not compress the vessel running between them. Never over a joint; it will not work.

Tighten until two things happen together: the bleeding stops, and the pulse below it disappears. Both. That is the endpoint, not a number of turns and not until it looks tight enough.

This matters because of a specific failure mode. A tourniquet tightened enough to compress veins but not arteries is worse than no tourniquet at all. Blood keeps arriving through the deeper, higher-pressure arteries and cannot get out through the compressed surface veins, so the limb engorges and bleeds harder. If you apply one and the bleeding increases, the answer is almost always to tighten it, not to take it off.

It will hurt. Properly applied tourniquets are genuinely painful, and patients ask for them to be loosened. That pain is expected and is not a reason to loosen anything. Tell them it is meant to hurt and that it is working.

Two things the receiving hospital needs. Never cover it — no blanket, no sleeve rolled down over it. Tourniquets get missed under blankets, with serious consequences. And write the time of application somewhere it cannot be lost: on the tourniquet itself if it has a panel, or on the patient's skin. The time drives every decision made about that limb afterwards.

Once it is on, leave it on. Do not release it, do not periodically loosen it, do not remove it because the bleeding appears to have stopped. Release is a hospital decision made with the ability to deal with what follows.

And if one does not control the bleeding, put a second one on just above the first. Two working together are frequently what a large thigh needs.
read.standard: Tourniquet application is indicated for life-threatening extremity haemorrhage uncontrolled by direct pressure, where direct pressure is impractical, and for traumatic amputation. Contemporary evidence, substantially derived from military experience, establishes that correctly applied tourniquets are safe for prolonged periods; historical concerns regarding limb loss reflected inadequate devices and prolonged application. Application is proximal to the wound, over a single long bone where anatomically possible, and never across a joint. Tightening continues until haemorrhage ceases and the distal pulse is abolished; both endpoints are required. Insufficient tightening occludes venous return without arresting arterial inflow, increasing haemorrhage; increased bleeding following application indicates the need for further tightening rather than removal. Pain is an expected consequence and does not indicate loosening. Tourniquets are never covered, and the application time is recorded visibly on the device or patient. Field release or intermittent loosening is contraindicated; release is a hospital decision. A second tourniquet is applied proximal to the first where one proves insufficient.

concepts.title: Wound packing and hemostatic dressings

It is not used for chest or abdominal wounds, where there is no floor to pack against
The principle is to fill the entire wound cavity tightly and then hold pressure on the packing
Pack directly onto the bleeding point: push the gauze deep, find the source, and keep feeding more in
A loosely packed wound does not work — the packing has to be tight enough to press the vessel closed from inside

read.plain:
Wound packing exists for the wounds a tourniquet cannot solve. If bleeding is coming from a limb, you use a tourniquet. If it is coming from where the limb meets the body — the groin, the armpit — or from the neck, there is nowhere to put a tourniquet, and packing is the answer.

First, where you do not pack. Not the chest. Not the abdomen. Those are cavities, not wounds with a floor, and packing gauze into them does nothing except push gauze into a cavity. Junctional wounds and deep wounds at the boundary of the torso are what this is for.

The principle is simple and the execution is brutal. You are filling the whole wound cavity tightly enough that the packing itself presses the bleeding vessel shut from inside.

That means going in. Put a finger into the wound, find the bleeding point, and pack directly onto it. Feed gauze in and keep feeding — far more than you expect, because these cavities are bigger than they look from outside. Push each addition down firmly and pack against the source, not just into the space around it.

A loosely packed wound is a failed packed wound. Gauze sitting in a cavity absorbs blood and does nothing. The pressure has to come from the packing being tight, and that means your fist and your body weight going into it.

Hemostatic gauze is impregnated with an agent that accelerates clotting. It goes in exactly the same way — the technique does not change because the gauze is clever. The agent shortens how long things take; it does not replace packing properly.

Then hold. Firm, direct pressure on the packed wound for whatever time your protocol or the product specifies — and hold for the whole time without letting go to check. Same principle as direct pressure, with higher stakes because you cannot start again easily.

Once it is packed, it stays packed. Do not remove it to look. Do not repack it because you are not sure. Secure it with a pressure dressing over the top and let the hospital deal with what is underneath.

One practical thing that is rarely said plainly: this hurts more than almost anything else you will do to a conscious patient. You are pushing gauze into an open wound with your fingers. They will not be able to keep still, however much they want to help. Get people positioned to hold them before you start, tell the patient what is about to happen, and then do it properly rather than gently. Doing it half-heartedly because it is distressing means doing it twice.
read.standard: Wound packing addresses junctional haemorrhage inaccessible to tourniquet application: inguinal, axillary, cervical and deep wounds at the torso boundary. Technique requires complete tight filling of the wound cavity such that the packing compresses the bleeding vessel internally. Gauze is introduced digitally onto the bleeding source and progressively fed into the cavity with firm downward pressure; cavity volume typically exceeds external appearance. Loose packing is ineffective, functioning only as absorbent material. Haemostatic gauze incorporates a clotting-accelerating agent and is packed by identical technique; the agent reduces required time but does not substitute for correct packing. Sustained direct pressure is maintained over the packed wound for the interval specified by protocol or product without interruption. Packing is not removed for inspection and is secured with a pressure dressing. The procedure produces severe pain; adequate personnel for patient restraint should be positioned before commencing.

eli_new.body: The mistake that ruins this is being gentle because it is distressing to do. A half-packed wound keeps bleeding and has to be done again, which hurts twice as much in total. Get help to hold them, warn the patient, and then commit.

concepts.title: Internal bleeding recognition
key_points: Internal bleeding cannot be seen, cannot be measured, and cannot be controlled by anything an EMT carries
It is recognised from the mechanism and from the signs of shock, not from anything visible
Suspect it from the mechanism: blunt abdominal trauma, a fall from height, a crash, penetrating torso injury, rib or pelvic fractures
Signs are the signs of shock: rising pulse, pale cool clammy skin, anxiety then confusion, thirst, and falling pressure late

read.plain:
Internal bleeding is the injury you cannot see, cannot measure, and cannot fix. That combination is what makes it dangerous, and it is why recognition is entirely about inference.

Start with where blood can go. A patient can lose an enormous volume into the abdominal cavity, into a chest cavity, into the pelvis after a pelvic fracture, and into the soft tissues of the thighs after femur fractures. Several litres, in some cases, with absolutely nothing visible from outside. The phrase worth remembering is that the floor and four more — the ground, chest, abdomen, pelvis, and long bones — are where the blood is when you cannot find it.

So you recognise it two ways: the mechanism, and the shock.

Mechanism first, because it comes before any sign. Blunt abdominal trauma. A fall from height. A significant crash, especially with compartment intrusion. Penetrating injury anywhere on the torso. Rib fractures, which mean force went into the chest. A suspected pelvic fracture. Any of those means you should be expecting internal bleeding rather than waiting to be shown it.

Then the shock findings, in the order they appear. A rising pulse first — the earliest sign and the most useful. Skin that goes pale, cool and clammy. A patient who becomes anxious and restless, then confused, then quiet. Thirst, which is a genuinely underrated finding. And blood pressure falling last, because the body defends it until it cannot any more.

That ordering is the whole art of this. A normal blood pressure does not mean no internal bleeding; it means compensation is still working. If you wait for the pressure to fall before you take it seriously, you are waiting for the point at which the patient is close to running out of reserve.

Local signs, when you have them, help. Abdominal tenderness, guarding, rigidity, distension. Bruising over the flank or around the navel. Pelvic instability — though you check that once, gently, and then not again.

But be careful with bruising. It takes hours to develop. Looking for it in the first hour and being reassured by smooth skin is a real error; the bruising that will be dramatic tomorrow is invisible now.

Blood coming up or out — coughed, vomited, or passed — tells you the gastrointestinal tract is involved and is as significant as anything you can see externally.

And the treatment is short, because almost nothing is yours. Oxygen as indicated. Keep them warm, because cold patients clot badly and a shocked patient loses heat fast. Position appropriately. Nothing by mouth, because they may go to theatre. And transport quickly to a surgeon, which is the only thing that is going to stop this. Do not spend scene time looking for a sign that confirms what the mechanism already told you.
read.standard: Internal haemorrhage is neither visible nor quantifiable prehospitally and is not controllable within EMT scope; recognition is inferential, derived from mechanism and shock findings. Major volume loss occurs into the thoracic cavity, peritoneal cavity, retroperitoneum and pelvis, and the soft tissues of the thigh following femoral fracture, without external evidence. Mechanisms conferring suspicion include blunt abdominal trauma, falls from height, vehicular trauma with compartment intrusion, penetrating torso injury, rib fractures and suspected pelvic fracture. Shock findings appear in sequence: tachycardia earliest, followed by pallor with cool clammy skin, anxiety progressing to confusion and obtundation, thirst, and hypotension as a late finding reflecting decompensation. Normotension therefore does not exclude significant haemorrhage. Local findings include abdominal tenderness, guarding, rigidity, distension, flank or periumbilical ecchymosis, and pelvic instability, assessed once only. Ecchymosis develops over hours and its early absence carries no exclusionary value. Haemoptysis, haematemesis and rectal bleeding indicate gastrointestinal involvement. Management comprises oxygen as indicated, active warming, positioning, nil by mouth and expedited transport for surgical haemorrhage control.

eli_new.analogy: The blood is on the floor, or in the chest, the abdomen, the pelvis, or the thighs. Those are the only places several litres can hide, and four of them are inside the patient.
eli_new.body: The trap is the blood pressure. It is the last thing to go and the first thing people look at. A rising pulse on a pale, clammy, anxious patient with a normal pressure is internal bleeding being compensated for, and that is the moment to act rather than the moment to be reassured.

concepts.title: Hemorrhagic shock
key_points: Shock is inadequate perfusion — not low blood pressure, which is only one late sign of it
Hemorrhagic shock is shock caused by blood loss, and the treatment is stopping the bleeding and replacing the blood
Compensated shock is the body maintaining pressure by speeding the heart and clamping down the vessels; the patient looks stable and is not

read.plain:
Shock is not low blood pressure. Shock is inadequate perfusion — tissue not getting the oxygen it needs. Low blood pressure is one sign of shock, and a late one. Defining shock by a number means you will only recognise it once it is well advanced, and a great deal of harm comes from exactly that.

Hemorrhagic shock is shock from blood loss. The treatment, ultimately, is to stop the bleeding and replace the blood. Hold that in mind because it tells you what your job is: everything you do is either stopping bleeding, protecting what circulation remains, or shortening the time to somebody who can do the rest.

There are two phases and the difference matters enormously.

Compensated shock is the body fighting back successfully. The heart speeds up. Vessels in the skin and the gut clamp down to push blood towards the brain and heart. The result is a patient with a fast pulse, pale cool clammy skin, some anxiety, and a blood pressure that is still normal. That is the whole problem. The number reads normal because the body is working extremely hard to keep it there, and a crew looking at the monitor sees stability that is not there.

Decompensated shock is when that fails. The pressure drops, the mental status falls, and the patient deteriorates quickly. It is late, it is ominous, and it means a substantial proportion of the blood volume is already gone.

Children deserve a specific warning. They compensate better than adults, they hold their pressure longer, and when it finally goes it goes fast, with very little warning. A normal blood pressure in a seriously injured child is close to meaningless as reassurance. Read the pulse, the skin, the capillary refill and the mental status instead.

So what can you actually do? Three things, and they are worth a great deal.

Stop external bleeding. Pressure, packing, tourniquets. This is the one you can genuinely fix.

Keep them warm. This sounds like comfort and it is not. Cold blood clots badly, and a shocked patient loses heat frighteningly fast — undressed, on a cold surface, with poor perfusion. Hypothermia, acidosis and impaired clotting reinforce each other in a cycle that is very hard to break once it is established. Blankets on a bleeding trauma patient are a clotting intervention.

And get them to a surgeon. The blood and the operation are the treatment and neither is on your vehicle.

Position supine unless their breathing will not tolerate it. Note that the old head-down position is no longer routinely recommended; the evidence did not support it and it has fallen out of practice. Check your protocol.

And nothing by mouth, however thirsty they are — and they will be thirsty, because thirst is a genuine sign of significant blood loss. Oxygen as indicated, handle them as little as possible, and pre-alert.
read.standard: Shock denotes inadequate tissue perfusion; hypotension constitutes a single late manifestation rather than a definition. Haemorrhagic shock arises from blood volume loss, with definitive management comprising haemorrhage control and blood replacement. Compensated shock reflects maintained perfusion pressure through tachycardia and peripheral vasoconstriction, producing tachycardia, pallor, cool clammy skin and anxiety with preserved blood pressure; apparent haemodynamic stability is misleading. Decompensated shock follows failure of compensatory mechanisms, with hypotension and deteriorating mental status, and indicates substantial volume loss. Paediatric patients compensate more effectively and decompensate abruptly; normotension carries minimal reassurance value and assessment relies on pulse, perfusion, capillary refill and mental status. EMT-level interventions comprise external haemorrhage control, prevention of hypothermia and expedited transport. Hypothermia impairs coagulation and, with acidosis, establishes a self-reinforcing cycle; active warming constitutes a coagulation intervention rather than a comfort measure. Supine positioning is used unless respiratory compromise precludes it; Trendelenburg positioning is no longer routinely recommended. Nil by mouth is maintained despite thirst, which itself indicates significant loss.

eli_new.analogy: Compensated shock is a patient sprinting to stand still. The blood pressure looks normal because of how hard they are working, and they cannot keep it up.
eli_new.body: Two habits worth more than anything technical. Stop defining shock by the blood pressure — read the pulse and the skin. And put blankets on bleeding patients, because cold blood does not clot and a cold trauma patient is a bleeding trauma patient who is getting worse.

read.plain:
Most nosebleeds come from a patch on the front of the septum where several small vessels meet, close to the surface and easily disturbed. Those are the ones you can fix on somebody's sofa, and they are the majority.

The technique is simple and almost always done wrong.

Sit them up and lean them forward. Forward, not back. The instinct — and the advice everyone's grandmother gave — is to tilt the head back, and it is wrong. It does not slow the bleeding; it just redirects it down the throat where you cannot see it. Swallowed blood is intensely irritating to the stomach, so the patient vomits, and now you have a vomiting patient with a nosebleed. Forward, over a bowl.

Pinch the soft part of the nose — the fleshy bit below the bone. People pinch the bridge, which is bone, and compresses nothing. Get your fingers below that, onto the soft cartilage, and squeeze firmly.

Then hold for at least ten minutes without releasing. Not squeezing, releasing to check, and squeezing again — that resets the clock every time, exactly as with any other bleeding. Ten full minutes, timed, and it is longer than it feels.

Do not pack the nose, and do not tilt the head back.

Ask about anticoagulants, because they change the picture: these bleeds are heavier, they last much longer, and they far more often need a hospital.

A posterior bleed comes from further back, and it declares itself in a particular way — the patient is positioned and pinched correctly, and there is very little coming out of the front, but blood is running down the back of their throat and they keep swallowing. That is a bleed you are not going to reach and it can be substantial. It needs hospital management.

Now the important exception. A nosebleed after significant head trauma is a different thing entirely. If there is clear or straw-coloured fluid mixed with the blood, that can be cerebrospinal fluid, which means a fracture at the base of the skull. Do not pack that nose. Do not pinch it closed. You would be obstructing drainage and pushing material towards the inside of the skull. Let it drain, cover loosely, and transport.

And do not dismiss a nosebleed as minor. Ongoing bleeding from a nose can produce genuine shock, particularly in an older patient on a blood thinner who has been bleeding steadily for an hour before anybody called. Take a pulse and look at the skin, as you would for bleeding anywhere else.
read.standard: Epistaxis most commonly originates from the anterior nasal septum and is amenable to simple measures. Management comprises upright seated positioning with forward inclination, directing blood externally rather than posteriorly; posterior drainage produces gastric irritation with emesis. Compression is applied to the soft cartilaginous portion rather than the bony dorsum, maintained continuously for a minimum of ten minutes without interruption for inspection. Nasal packing and head extension are contraindicated. Anticoagulation produces heavier and more protracted bleeding with greater likelihood of requiring hospital intervention. Posterior epistaxis presents with minimal anterior bleeding despite correct technique alongside continuous posterior drainage and repeated swallowing, and requires hospital management. Epistaxis following significant head trauma, particularly with clear or serosanguineous fluid suggesting cerebrospinal fluid, indicates possible basilar skull fracture; nasal packing and compression are contraindicated, with loose covering and transport indicated. Sustained epistaxis may produce haemorrhagic shock, particularly in geriatric and anticoagulated patients.

eli_new.analogy: Leaning back does not stop a nosebleed. It hides it, in a stomach, and gives it back to you ten minutes later as vomit.
eli_new.body: Two errors, both nearly universal. Tilting the head back, which sends the blood down the throat. And pinching the bony bridge, which compresses nothing at all. Forward, and on the soft part.

read.plain:
A closed injury is damage under skin that has not broken. That is what makes them deceptive — there is nothing to see, and nothing to see is frequently read as nothing wrong.

A contusion is a bruise. Small vessels tear, blood leaks into the tissue, and you get swelling, tenderness and eventually discolouration. A hematoma is the same process on a larger scale and collected in one place, and a big one — in a thigh, say — can hold a genuinely significant volume of blood.

And here is the point that keeps coming up in trauma: bruising appears late. Hours. The impressive purple bruise is tomorrow's finding, not today's. So looking at smooth unmarked skin an hour after a serious impact and concluding that not much happened is a real error.

Crush injury is the serious one in this concept, and its danger is counterintuitive.

When a limb is compressed for a prolonged period, the muscle inside it dies. While the pressure is on, the products of that dying muscle are trapped locally — the patient may be talking to you, in pain but stable, for a long time.

The danger arrives when the pressure comes off. Circulation returns, and everything that accumulated in that limb washes into the general circulation at once: potassium, acid, and the breakdown products of muscle. Potassium can stop a heart. The breakdown products can block the kidneys. Patients have arrested at the moment of release, having been stable and conversational under the weight for an hour.

What that means for you is practical. If a patient has been trapped for a prolonged period, tell the rescue team that the release is a clinical event, not just an extrication milestone. Everybody should be ready for it, at the patient's side, before the weight comes off. Advanced treatments exist and are not yours, so if release is imminent and the entrapment has been long, a paramedic or a physician should be there if that is possible in your system.

Compartment syndrome is the other complication worth knowing. Muscles sit in compartments wrapped in tough sheets of tissue that do not stretch. Swelling inside a compartment raises the pressure until it exceeds the pressure in the small vessels, and the muscle inside begins to die — with the skin intact and the limb looking unremarkable.

The warning sign is pain out of proportion to the injury. A patient whose pain seems excessive for what you can see is not exaggerating; that disproportion is the classic finding. Pain on passive stretching of the muscles, a tight woody feel to the compartment, and later numbness and tingling complete the picture. A pulse may still be present — losing the pulse is very late and its presence is no reassurance.

For simple closed injuries: cold, and check circulation, sensation and movement below the injury. And record what you find, because someone will want to know whether it changed.
read.standard: Closed soft tissue injury denotes damage beneath intact integument, with severity readily underestimated. Contusion comprises capillary disruption with interstitial haemorrhage producing swelling, tenderness and delayed discolouration; haematoma denotes a localised collection which may sequester substantial volume. Ecchymosis develops over hours, and early absence carries no exclusionary value regarding force sustained. Crush injury results from prolonged tissue compression with resultant rhabdomyolysis; the critical period follows decompression rather than accompanying compression, as restored circulation releases accumulated potassium, acid and myoglobin systemically, precipitating dysrhythmia and renal failure. Prolonged entrapment therefore requires that release be treated as a clinical event, with appropriate personnel present and, where available, advanced-level attendance. Compartment syndrome arises from raised intracompartmental pressure exceeding capillary perfusion pressure within inelastic fascial boundaries, producing muscle necrosis despite intact skin and unremarkable appearance. The cardinal finding is pain disproportionate to apparent injury, with pain on passive stretch, tense compartment, and later paraesthesia; preserved distal pulses do not exclude it and pulselessness is a late finding. Management of simple closed injury comprises cold application and documented neurovascular assessment distal to the injury.

eli_new.analogy: A crushed limb under a weight is a sealed container. The emergency starts when somebody opens it.
eli_new.body: Two things to carry away. Pain out of proportion to the injury is a finding, not a personality trait — it is the earliest sign of compartment syndrome. And a long-trapped limb being freed is a moment to be standing next to the patient, not a moment to relax.

story.title: Before you lift it
story.dispatch: Engine 6 — worker trapped under machinery, conscious, one leg pinned, 70 minutes.

He had been talking the whole time, in pain but entirely stable, and the rescue crew were ready to lift.

The medic asked them to wait two minutes so everybody could be in position at the patient rather than at the machine.

The hour under the weight was survivable. The moment it came off was the part that needed everybody watching.

concepts.title: Open injuries and impaled objects
key_points: Abrasion scrapes off the surface layers: painful, often dirty, rarely serious in itself
Laceration is a cut, which may be clean-edged or ragged, and can be deep enough to involve vessels, nerves and tendons
Avulsion is a flap of tissue torn loose but still attached; the flap is replaced in its normal position and dressed
Amputation is complete separation of a part, and the stump is controlled with pressure or a tourniquet
Penetrating and puncture wounds may look trivial and be deep, and the entry size means nothing
An impaled object is stabilised in place and never removed — it may be tamponading a vessel, and removing it releases the bleeding
The exceptions to leaving an impaled object are when it obstructs the airway or prevents chest compressions
Stabilise an impaled object with bulky dressings built up around it, and control bleeding around the base
Check circulation, sensation and movement distal to any open wound, and record it before and after dressing
misconceptions: Removing an impaled object
Pushing an avulsed flap aside rather than replacing it
Being reassured by the small size of a puncture wound
Failing to document neurovascular status before dressing
exam_favorites: Never remove an impaled object and the two exceptions

read.plain:
Open wounds are classified by what happened to the tissue, and the classification is useful because each type has a different practical consequence.

An abrasion is a scrape — the surface layers rubbed off. They are painful out of proportion to their depth because the nerve endings are exposed, and they are often dirty, with grit and road material ground in.

A laceration is a cut. Clean-edged from glass or a blade, ragged from a tearing force. The thing to remember is that depth matters more than length: a short deep laceration can involve a vessel, a nerve or a tendon.

An avulsion is a flap of tissue torn loose but still attached at one edge. The right thing to do is gently replace the flap into its normal position and dress it there. That flap often has a blood supply through its attachment, and a replaced flap can survive. Do not fold it back or leave it hanging.

Amputation is complete separation. Control the stump with direct pressure and, if that fails, a tourniquet. The part itself has its own concept.

Puncture and penetrating wounds are the deceptive category. A nail, a blade, a spike — a tiny external mark over a deep track. Never judge these by the size of the hole, and always ask what went in and how far.

Now the rule this concept is built around: an impaled object stays where it is.

The reason is mechanical. That object may be pressing against the vessel it damaged on the way in, and sitting there holding the bleeding closed. Pull it out and you remove the plug. Bleeding that was controlled becomes uncontrolled, and now you have a wound with no way to reach the source. You also cause fresh damage on the way out, because objects do not retrace their path.

So stabilise it. Build bulky dressings up around the object so it cannot move, and secure them so the object is supported rather than the object supporting itself. Movement during transport tears more tissue.

Control bleeding around the base with pressure applied beside the object, not on it.

There are two exceptions, and both are situations where the object prevents something immediately life-saving. If it is in the cheek and obstructing the airway, or if it is in the chest in a way that makes chest compressions impossible, it comes out. Those are the only two. If you are considering removal for any other reason, the answer is no.

And for every open wound, check circulation, sensation and movement below it — before you dress it and again afterwards. That record is what tells the hospital whether something changed while the patient was in your care.
read.standard: Open soft tissue injuries are classified by mechanism. Abrasion denotes superficial epidermal removal, disproportionately painful owing to nerve ending exposure and frequently contaminated. Laceration denotes incision with clean or irregular margins; depth rather than length determines involvement of vascular, neural and tendinous structures. Avulsion denotes a tissue flap detached but retaining attachment; the flap is repositioned anatomically and dressed in situ, preserving perfusion through the pedicle. Amputation denotes complete separation, with stump haemorrhage controlled by direct pressure or tourniquet. Puncture and penetrating wounds present minimal external evidence with potentially extensive tracts; external dimensions carry no prognostic value. Impaled objects are stabilised in situ and not removed, as the object may tamponade the vessel it disrupted and removal produces uncontrolled haemorrhage inaccessible to direct control, together with additional tissue damage along a divergent path. Stabilisation employs bulky dressings built around the object; haemorrhage is controlled by pressure adjacent to rather than upon the object. Removal is indicated only where the object obstructs the airway or precludes chest compressions. Neurovascular status distal to any open wound is assessed and documented before and after dressing.

eli_new.analogy: An impaled object is often the only thing holding the bleeding closed. Pulling it out is removing a plug from a hole you cannot then reach.
eli_new.body: The two exceptions to leaving an impaled object are narrow and specific: it blocks the airway, or it stops chest compressions. Anything else — it is awkward, it will not fit in the ambulance, the patient wants it out — is not an exception.

story.title: It won't fit
story.dispatch: Engine 9 — male impaled on railings, conscious, bleeding controlled.

The immediate practical problem was that the railing was a metre long and the patient could not be moved with it attached.

Somebody asked whether they could just pull him off it, and the answer was no, and the fire crew cut the railing instead.

Awkward is not one of the exceptions. There are only two, and neither of them is about whether it fits in the ambulance.

concepts.title: Dressing and bandaging principles
key_points: A dressing covers the wound; a bandage holds the dressing in place — two different things with two different jobs
Dressings should be sterile where possible and large enough to cover the whole wound with a margin
Bandages are applied firmly enough to secure and to apply pressure, but never so tight that they cut off circulation
Check circulation, sensation and movement distal to any bandage after applying it, and again during transport
Swelling continues after you leave, so a bandage that was correct on scene can become a tourniquet by the hospital
Bandage from distal to proximal on a limb so that you push fluid towards the body rather than trapping it
Leave fingers and toes exposed where possible so circulation can be checked without undoing anything
Never bandage circumferentially around the neck
An occlusive dressing is used where air must be kept out: open chest wounds, large neck wounds, and eviscerations
misconceptions: Applying a bandage so tight it compromises circulation
Covering fingertips so circulation cannot be checked
Failing to reassess after swelling develops
Bandaging around the neck
exam_favorites: When an occlusive dressing is used

read.plain:
Two words that get used interchangeably and should not be. A dressing goes on the wound; its job is to cover, absorb and protect. A bandage goes over the dressing; its job is to hold it there and, when needed, to apply pressure.

Dressings should be sterile where you can manage it, and big enough to cover the whole wound with a margin. A dressing the same size as the wound leaves the edges exposed and slides off centre the moment anybody moves.

Bandages need to be firm enough to do their job and no firmer. That sounds obvious and it is the single most common error in this whole area, for a specific reason.

The reason is swelling. You apply a bandage on scene, it is snug and correct, and then over the next forty minutes the injured tissue swells underneath it. A bandage that was right when you applied it can be a tourniquet by the time you arrive. This is why the rule is not just to check circulation after applying it, but to check it again during transport. The first check tells you that you did it right. The second tells you whether it is still right.

So: after every bandage, check circulation, sensation and movement below it. Colour, warmth, capillary refill, pulse if you can find one, whether they can feel you touching and whether they can move. And do it again on the way.

A few practical rules. On a limb, bandage from the far end towards the body. That way you are moving fluid towards the circulation rather than trapping it out at the fingertips.

Leave the fingers and toes uncovered whenever the injury allows. That way you can check circulation at a glance without undoing your own work. Covering the fingertips means every reassessment costs you a rebandage, which means reassessments quietly stop happening.

Never bandage all the way around a neck. It should not need saying and it gets done.

And occlusive dressings, which are a different tool for a different problem. An occlusive dressing does not breathe — its purpose is to stop air getting in. You use one where air entering would harm the patient: an open chest wound, where air drawn into the chest collapses the lung; a large wound in the neck where air could enter a vein; and over an evisceration, where a moist dressing covered with an occlusive layer keeps exposed bowel from drying out. Those are the situations. Ordinary wounds get ordinary dressings.
read.standard: A dressing covers the wound, providing coverage, absorption and protection; a bandage secures the dressing and may provide compression. Dressings should be sterile where practicable and sufficiently large to cover the wound with a surrounding margin. Bandages are applied with sufficient firmness for security and compression without compromising perfusion. Neurovascular status distal to any bandage is assessed following application and reassessed during transport, as progressive tissue oedema may convert an appropriately applied bandage into an occlusive constriction. Limb bandaging proceeds distal to proximal, directing fluid towards the central circulation. Digits are left exposed where injury permits, enabling perfusion assessment without disturbing the dressing. Circumferential cervical bandaging is contraindicated. Occlusive dressings, being impermeable to air, are indicated where air entry would cause harm: open thoracic wounds, large cervical wounds with venous air embolism risk, and evisceration, where a moist dressing covered by an occlusive layer prevents desiccation of exposed viscera.

eli_new.analogy: A bandage is a snapshot of how swollen the limb was when you applied it. The limb keeps swelling; the bandage does not keep growing.
eli_new.body: Leave the fingertips out. It sounds trivial and it is the difference between reassessing circulation five times on the way in, and reassessing it once because each check means undoing everything.

story.title: It was fine when we put it on
story.dispatch: Handover — forearm laceration, bandaged at scene, 40 minute transport.
story.body:
The bandage had been applied correctly and the fingers had been pink and warm when they left.

Nobody looked again, because the fingertips had been covered up and checking meant undoing it.

At handover the hand was dusky. Nothing had been done wrong on scene. The swelling had simply carried on happening.

concepts.title: Amputated part care
key_points: The patient always takes priority over the part: control the stump bleeding first
Control the stump with direct pressure, and a tourniquet if pressure fails
Wrap the amputated part in a dry sterile dressing, place it in a sealed plastic bag, and put that bag on ice or in cold water
The part must never touch ice directly and must never be frozen, because freezing destroys the tissue and ends any chance of reattachment
Do not soak the part in water, and do not use dry ice
Bring the part with the patient, and if it cannot be found immediately, transport the patient anyway and have the part follow
A partial amputation is not completed — the remaining attachment may carry the blood supply, so it is supported in position and dressed
Label the part and note the time of amputation
Handle the part gently and do not clean or scrub it
misconceptions: Putting the amputated part directly on ice, or freezing it
Delaying transport of the patient to search for the part
Completing a partial amputation
Soaking the part in water or antiseptic

read.plain:
There are two things at an amputation: a patient and a part. They are not equally important, and the ordering trips people up because the part is dramatic and attracts attention.

The patient comes first. Control the stump. Direct pressure, firm and focused, and if that does not work, a tourniquet without hesitating — amputation is a textbook tourniquet indication. Get the bleeding stopped before anybody starts thinking about the part.

Then the part, and the handling matters because it determines whether reattachment is even possible.

Wrap it in a dry sterile dressing. Put the wrapped part in a sealed plastic bag. Put the sealed bag on ice, or in cold water with ice in it.

The critical detail is that the part never touches ice directly, and is never frozen. Freezing kills the tissue outright, and a frozen part cannot be reattached to anything. The bag is what stands between the tissue and the ice. Cool is the goal; frozen is the end of it. And no dry ice, ever — far too cold.

Do not soak the part in water. Do not put it in antiseptic. Do not clean or scrub it. Do not pick bits off it. Wrap it, bag it, cool it, and let the surgeons deal with what is on it.

Bring it with the patient. If the part cannot be found straight away — and at industrial and road incidents that is common — do not hold the patient on scene searching for it. The patient is the emergency. Transport, and arrange for the part to follow with the fire crew or the police once it is found. A part arriving twenty minutes later is far better than a patient arriving twenty minutes later.

Partial amputations need their own rule, and it is important: you do not complete them. However badly attached the part looks, whatever strand of tissue is holding it, that attachment may be carrying the blood supply that is keeping the distal tissue alive. Support the part in the position it is in, dress it, splint the limb so nothing twists or drags during movement, and leave it attached.

And label the part with the patient's name and the time of the amputation, because those two facts determine what the receiving team can attempt.
read.standard: Management prioritises the patient over the amputated part. Stump haemorrhage is controlled by direct pressure, with tourniquet application where pressure fails; amputation constitutes a primary tourniquet indication. The amputated part is wrapped in dry sterile dressing, placed within a sealed plastic bag, and the bag cooled on ice or in iced water. Direct contact between tissue and ice is contraindicated, as is freezing, which produces irreversible tissue destruction precluding replantation; dry ice is contraindicated. Immersion in water or antiseptic, and cleaning or debridement of the part, are contraindicated. The part accompanies the patient where available; where the part cannot be immediately located, patient transport proceeds without delay and the part follows separately. Partial amputations are not completed, as the residual attachment may convey perfusion to distal tissue; the part is supported in position, dressed and the limb splinted to prevent traction or torsion. The part is labelled with patient identification and the time of amputation.

eli_new.analogy: Cool, not cold. The bag is the boundary between saving the part and destroying it, and ice touching tissue is on the wrong side of that boundary.
eli_new.body: Two absolutes. Never freeze the part, and never complete a partial amputation. Both are done with good intentions — packing it well in ice, tidying up something barely attached — and both end any chance of that limb being reattached.

story.title: Packed in ice
story.dispatch: Handover — industrial amputation, part recovered by the fire crew.
story.body:
Everybody had done well. The stump was controlled, the patient was stable, and somebody had thoughtfully surrounded the part with ice to keep it as cold as possible.

It had been in direct contact with the ice for thirty-five minutes.

Cool preserves tissue. Frozen destroys it, and the plastic bag was the only thing that was ever going to separate the two.

concepts.title: Burn depth classification
key_points: Burn depth describes how far through the skin the damage goes, and it determines healing, scarring and whether surgery is needed
Superficial burns involve only the outer layer: red, dry, painful, no blisters — sunburn is the everyday example
Partial thickness burns go through the outer layer into the dermis: blistered, moist, mottled red or pink, and intensely painful
Full thickness burns destroy all layers: white, leathery, waxy or charred, dry, and typically painless in the burned area
That painlessness is the key finding — the nerve endings have been destroyed, so the worst burns hurt least
A full thickness burn is almost always surrounded by partial thickness burn, so the patient still has pain from the edges
Burns are frequently mixed depth, and depth can be hard to judge early and may declare itself over the following days
Superficial burns are excluded when calculating burn extent for fluid decisions; partial and full thickness are counted
A circumferential full thickness burn around a limb or the chest can constrict like a tourniquet as swelling develops

Counting superficial burns in the extent calculation
